text:
**Short answer: Starling is the safest all-round pick for a main UK account.** Choose **Chase** if cashback and savings are your priorities; choose **Revolut** if you’ll make frequent foreign-currency payments and want its extra app features.

| | **Starling** | **Chase** | **Revolut** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Best for** | Everyday banking and reliability | Cashback and saving | Travel, currencies and app features |
| **Main-account strengths** | Straightforward current account, no monthly fee, fee-free spending and cash withdrawals abroad; overdrafts available if approved | No account fee; no-fee spending abroad; current cashback offer can be valuable if you meet its conditions | Broad currency and travel features; UK current-account deposits are now FSCS-protected once held with Revolut Bank |
| **Main caveat** | No headline cashback; overdrafts are interest-bearing | Cashback is conditional and capped; check the current eligibility rules | Check which Revolut account and terms apply to you, particularly during the transition to its UK bank |

### My take

- **Starling** is the best default if you want one account for salary, bills, Direct Debits and day-to-day spending. It’s a full current account, has no monthly fee, and has a useful overdraft option—though rates vary by customer.
- **Chase** could be better value if you regularly spend in its cashback categories. Its current offer advertises **2% cashback up to £20 a month**, but eligibility conditions apply. It’s also worth comparing its saver rate with alternatives before moving savings over.
- **Revolut** is attractive if you often use multiple currencies or want its travel and budgeting tools. It is now a UK-licensed bank, and eligible deposits in a Revolut Bank UK account are FSCS-protected up to **£120,000**. Still, confirm your account has been moved to the bank and which terms govern it.

**Bottom line:** If you want one choice without a special use case, I’d pick **Starling**. If you’ll reliably qualify for Chase’s cashback, **Chase** may pay you more. Either way, keeping a second account elsewhere as a backup is sensible.
